lines.text: Someone mailed him a steel box bolted shut with a coffee can welded inside.
ai: a rusty steel box bolted shut on a workbench with dramatic light

lines.text: And inside is a can of 1950s motor oil so would it still protect an engine?
ai: an old rusty vintage motor oil can from the 1950s on a shelf

lines.text: He cooks it at 410 degrees right next to modern oil.
ai: two glass beakers of motor oil heating on a glowing hot plate

lines.text: And the old oil loses 42 percent more weight so it's literally cooking off into the air.
ai: golden motor oil steaming and evaporating into the air
wisps of smoke rising from hot oil in slow motion

lines.text: In a minus forty freezer it barely moves.
ai: thick frozen motor oil covered in frost

lines.text: And after an engine run the cylinder head is crusty because oil that can't take heat bakes onto hot metal.
ai: a crusty black engine cylinder head macro
oil baking onto hot metal with smoke

lines.text: The lab report shows why because there's just 6 parts per million of calcium.
ai: a lab report sheet on a clipboard next to test tubes of oil

lines.text: Calcium is the detergent that grabs soot and acid so without it everything turns to sludge.

thick black sludge dripping inside an engine

lines.text: And its acid fighting reserve is zero point four versus six point two for modern oil which is fifteen times less.
ai: a nearly empty battery shaped glass of oil

lines.text: So it still lubricates but it's like a shield that's already used up and your engine would sludge fast.
ai: a cracked used up metal shield on a dark floor

lines.text: So would you put it in your car?
